domainDescription: The Builder track. Design a medical research database that cannot lie: schemas, constraints, transactions, triggers — and the cleanup of a very dirty legacy import.

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Welcome to MedCore Research. Day one: create the `patients` registry — a table with `patient_id` (INTEGER, the PRIMARY KEY), `full_name` (TEXT) and `age` (INTEGER).

hints.tier1Concept: CREATE TABLE defines a new table. Each column gets a name and a type; PRIMARY KEY marks the column that uniquely identifies each row.
hints.tier3Solution: CREATE TABLE patients (patient_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, full_name TEXT, age INTEGER);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT name, type, pk FROM pragma_table_info('patients') ORDER BY cid;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Our first volunteer signed up. Insert patient 1: Maya Okonkwo, age 34.

hints.tier1Concept: INSERT INTO adds a row. List the columns, then VALUES with one value per column. Text values go in single quotes.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, full_name, age)
VALUES (1, '___', ___);
hints.tier3Solution: INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, full_name, age) VALUES (1, 'Maya Okonkwo', 34);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT patient_id, full_name, age FROM patients;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Three more volunteers in one go — use a single INSERT with multiple value tuples: (2, 'Ahmed Haddad', 47), (3, 'Lena Berg', 29), (4, 'Carlos Reyes', 52).

hints.tier1Concept: One INSERT can add many rows: separate each (…) tuple with commas. Far faster than one statement per row.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, full_name, age) VALUES
  (2, 'Ahmed Haddad', 47),
  (3, ___, ___),
  (4, ___, ___);
hints.tier3Solution: INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, full_name, age) VALUES (2, 'Ahmed Haddad', 47), (3, 'Lena Berg', 29), (4, 'Carlos Reyes', 52);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT patient_id, full_name, age FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The trial protocol only covers volunteers over 40. Show the `full_name` and `age` of every patient older than 40.

hints.tier1Concept: SELECT picks columns; WHERE filters rows with a condition. Comparison operators: >, <, >=, <=, =, <>.
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT full_name, age FROM patients WHERE age > 40;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT full_name, age FROM patients WHERE age > 40;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Data-entry slip: Ahmed Haddad (patient 2) is 44, not 47. Correct his age — and only his.

hints.tier1Concept: UPDATE changes existing rows. The WHERE clause decides which rows change; without it, EVERY row is updated.
hints.tier3Solution: UPDATE patients SET age = 44 WHERE patient_id = 2;

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT patient_id, age FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Carlos Reyes (patient 4) withdrew consent. Remove his row from the registry.

hints.tier1Concept: DELETE FROM removes rows matching WHERE. Like UPDATE, an unscoped DELETE wipes the whole table — always write the WHERE first.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
DELETE FROM patients
WHERE patient_id = ___;
hints.tier3Solution: DELETE FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 4;

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, MAX(patient_id) AS mx FROM patients;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Compliance wants contact details. Add an `email` column (TEXT) to `patients`.

hints.tier1Concept: ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN evolves a table that already holds data. Existing rows get NULL for the new column.
hints.tier2Scaffold: ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN ___ ___;
hints.tier3Solution: ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN email TEXT;

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS cols, SUM(CASE WHEN name='email' AND type='TEXT' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_email FROM pragma_table_info('patients');

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Two more fields before the big import: add `site` (TEXT) and `enrolled_on` (TEXT) to `patients`. SQLite takes one ADD COLUMN per statement — submit both statements together, separated by a semicolon.

hints.tier1Concept: You can submit several SQL statements at once; each ends with a semicolon. SQLite's ALTER TABLE adds one column at a time.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN site TEXT;
ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN ___ ___;
hints.tier3Solution:
ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN site TEXT;
ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN enrolled_on TEXT;

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS cols, SUM(CASE WHEN name IN ('site','enrolled_on') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS new_cols FROM pragma_table_info('patients');

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Create the `sites` table where bad data is impossible: `site_id` (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY), `city` (TEXT NOT NULL), and `capacity` (INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 50).

hints.tier1Concept: NOT NULL rejects rows missing a value; DEFAULT fills the column automatically when the INSERT omits it. Constraints are how a schema defends itself.
hints.tier3Solution: CREATE TABLE sites (site_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT NOT NULL, capacity INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 50);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT name, "notnull" AS nn, dflt_value AS dv FROM pragma_table_info('sites') ORDER BY cid;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Consent records are legally binding — the status can only ever be GRANTED or REVOKED. Create `consents` with `consent_id` (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY), `patient_id` (INTEGER NOT NULL), and `status` (TEXT NOT NULL) with a CHECK that status is one of those two values.

hints.tier1Concept: A CHECK constraint is a rule every row must satisfy. CHECK (status IN ('A','B')) makes invalid states unrepresentable — the database rejects them at write time.
hints.tier3Solution: CREATE TABLE consents (consent_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, patient_id INTEGER NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('GRANTED','REVOKED')));

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_table_info('consents')) AS cols, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sqlite_master WHERE name='consents' AND sql LIKE '%CHECK%') AS has_check;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Register our five sites: (1, 'Geneva', 120), (2, 'Boston', 80), (3, 'Mumbai', 150), (4, 'Lagos', 90) in one INSERT — and for (5, 'Osaka'), use a second INSERT listing only site_id and city so the capacity DEFAULT does its job.

hints.tier1Concept: When an INSERT omits a column, SQLite applies its DEFAULT. You can mix a multi-row INSERT and a column-subset INSERT in one submission.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
INSERT INTO sites (site_id, city, capacity) VALUES (1,'Geneva',120), (2,'Boston',80), (3,'Mumbai',150), (4,'Lagos',90);
INSERT INTO sites (site_id, city) VALUES (5, ___);
hints.tier3Solution:
INSERT INTO sites (site_id, city, capacity) VALUES (1,'Geneva',120), (2,'Boston',80), (3,'Mumbai',150), (4,'Lagos',90);
INSERT INTO sites (site_id, city) VALUES (5, 'Osaka');

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT site_id, city, capacity FROM sites ORDER BY site_id;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Overnight, IT migrated the legacy registry into your `patients` table — hundreds of rows of… questionable quality. First: how many patients are in the table now? Return a single count.

hints.tier1Concept: COUNT(*) counts rows. It's the first thing to run after any bulk import — does the volume even look right?
hints.tier2Scaffold: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ___;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM patients;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM patients;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The migration didn't deduplicate contacts. Find every email used by MORE than one patient: return the `email` and how many patients share it. Ignore NULL and empty-string emails.

hints.tier1Concept: GROUP BY collapses rows per group; HAVING filters the groups AFTER aggregation (WHERE filters rows before).
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM patients
WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND email <> ''
GROUP BY ___
HAVING COUNT(*) ___;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n FROM patients WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND email <> '' GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n FROM patients WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND email <> '' GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: A colleague wrote this query to count patients with a missing email — it returns 0, which is clearly wrong. Fix it. (Missing means NULL or an empty string.)

hints.tier1Concept: NULL is not a value — it's the absence of one. `email = NULL` is never true (it's NULL), so the filter matches nothing. Use IS NULL.
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS missing_email FROM patients WHERE email IS NULL OR email = '';

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS missing_email FROM patients WHERE email IS NULL OR email = '';

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The outreach team needs a contact list that never shows blanks. For the 10 lowest patient_ids, return `patient_id` and the email — but substitute 'no-contact' when it is NULL or empty. Order by patient_id.

hints.tier1Concept: COALESCE(a, b, …) returns the first non-NULL argument. Pair it with NULLIF(email, '') to also catch empty strings: NULLIF returns NULL when its two arguments are equal.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT patient_id, COALESCE(NULLIF(email, ''), ___) AS contact
FROM patients
ORDER BY patient_id
LIMIT 10;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT patient_id, COALESCE(NULLIF(email, ''), 'no-contact') AS contact FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id LIMIT 10;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT patient_id, COALESCE(NULLIF(email, ''), 'no-contact') AS contact FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id LIMIT 10;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Some imported names carry leading or trailing whitespace — a classic legacy-system gift. Clean ALL names in place with TRIM.

hints.tier1Concept: String functions can be used inside UPDATE … SET to clean a whole column in one statement. TRIM strips leading/trailing spaces.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
UPDATE patients
SET full_name = TRIM(___);
hints.tier3Solution: UPDATE patients SET full_name = TRIM(full_name);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS dirty FROM patients WHERE full_name LIKE ' %' OR full_name LIKE '% ';

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The import created literal duplicate people — same name, age and site under different ids. Delete every duplicate, keeping the row with the LOWEST patient_id in each group.

hints.tier1Concept: The classic dedupe: keep MIN(id) per group, delete everything whose id is not in that set. (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY …) is the windowed variant.)
hints.tier3Solution: DELETE FROM patients WHERE patient_id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(patient_id) FROM patients GROUP BY full_name, age, site);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS dup_groups FROM (SELECT 1 FROM patients GROUP BY full_name, age, site HAVING COUNT(*) > 1);

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Several imported ages are biologically impossible (above 120). Don't guess — set those ages to NULL so they read as 'unknown' instead of wrong.

hints.tier1Concept: Setting a column to NULL is how you record 'we don't know'. An impossible value is worse than a missing one — it silently poisons averages.
hints.tier3Solution: UPDATE patients SET age = NULL WHERE age > 120;

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS impossible FROM patients WHERE age > 120;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Now that the data is clean, profile each site: return `site`, the patient count, and the average age rounded to 1 decimal (AVG skips NULL ages automatically).

hints.tier1Concept: Aggregates ignore NULLs — AVG(age) averages only known ages. ROUND(x, 1) keeps reports readable.
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT site, COUNT(*) AS patients, ROUND(AVG(age), 1) AS avg_age FROM patients GROUP BY site;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT site, COUNT(*) AS patients, ROUND(AVG(age), 1) AS avg_age FROM patients GROUP BY site;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Enrollment trend time. Count enrollments per calendar month: return the month as 'YYYY-MM' and the count, ordered by month.

hints.tier1Concept: strftime('%Y-%m', date_col) extracts a sortable month bucket from an ISO date string — the backbone of time-series reporting in SQLite.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS enrolled
FROM patients
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY ___;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS enrolled FROM patients GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS enrolled FROM patients GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Visits start next week. Create `visits`: `visit_id` (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY), `patient_id` (INTEGER NOT NULL referencing patients(patient_id)), `visit_on` (TEXT NOT NULL), `systolic` (INTEGER), `weight_kg` (REAL), `notes` (TEXT).

hints.tier1Concept: REFERENCES parent(col) declares a foreign key: a visit can only point at a patient that exists. With PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON (it is, here), SQLite enforces it.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
CREATE TABLE visits (
  visit_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  patient_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ___(___),
  visit_on TEXT NOT NULL,
  systolic INTEGER,
  weight_kg REAL,
  notes TEXT
);
hints.tier3Solution: CREATE TABLE visits (visit_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, patient_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES patients(patient_id), visit_on TEXT NOT NULL, systolic INTEGER, weight_kg REAL, notes TEXT);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_table_info('visits')) AS cols, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_foreign_key_list('visits')) AS fks;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: A thousand visit records just landed. Denormalize for the dashboard: add a `last_visit` (TEXT) column to patients, then fill it with each patient's most recent `visit_on` using a correlated subquery. Submit both statements together.

hints.tier1Concept: An UPDATE can SET a column from a subquery that references the outer row — a correlated subquery runs once per patient.
hints.tier3Solution:
ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN last_visit TEXT;
UPDATE patients SET last_visit = (SELECT MAX(visit_on) FROM visits WHERE visits.patient_id = patients.patient_id);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_table_info('patients') WHERE name='last_visit') AS has_col, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM patients p WHERE last_visit IS NOT (SELECT MAX(visit_on) FROM visits v WHERE v.patient_id = p.patient_id)) AS stale;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The print report wants whole numbers. Return the average systolic blood pressure across all visits, CAST to an INTEGER.

hints.tier1Concept: CAST(expr AS INTEGER) converts types explicitly. AVG returns a REAL; casting truncates toward zero — different from ROUND, and worth knowing which one you want.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT CAST(AVG(systolic) AS ___) AS avg_systolic
FROM visits;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT CAST(AVG(systolic) AS INTEGER) AS avg_systolic FROM visits;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT CAST(AVG(systolic) AS INTEGER) AS avg_systolic FROM visits;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The dedupe must never be needed again. Create a UNIQUE index `uq_patient_identity` on patients(full_name, age, site) so duplicate people are rejected at insert time.

hints.tier1Concept: A UNIQUE index is both a constraint and an index: it rejects duplicate key tuples AND speeds up lookups on those columns.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_patient_identity
ON patients(___, ___, ___);
hints.tier3Solution: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_patient_identity ON patients(full_name, age, site);

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS idx FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='index' AND name='uq_patient_identity' AND sql LIKE '%UNIQUE%';

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Who are we seeing most? Return the 5 patients with the most visits: `patient_id` and `visit_count`, ordered by visit_count descending, then patient_id ascending to break ties.

hints.tier1Concept: Top-N queries need a DETERMINISTIC order: always add a tiebreaker column, or two runs of the same query can return different rows.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT patient_id, COUNT(*) AS visit_count
FROM visits
GROUP BY patient_id
ORDER BY visit_count DESC, patient_id ASC
LIMIT ___;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT patient_id, COUNT(*) AS visit_count FROM visits GROUP BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_count DESC, patient_id ASC LIMIT 5;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT patient_id, COUNT(*) AS visit_count FROM visits GROUP BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_count DESC, patient_id ASC LIMIT 5;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Consent paperwork for patients 1 and 2 cleared legal — both must be recorded together or not at all. Inside a single transaction (BEGIN … COMMIT), insert consents (1, 1, 'GRANTED') and (2, 2, 'GRANTED').

hints.tier1Concept: A transaction makes several statements atomic: either every one commits, or none do. BEGIN starts it; COMMIT makes it permanent.

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT consent_id, patient_id, status FROM consents ORDER BY consent_id;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Rehearse the disaster drill: BEGIN a transaction, DELETE every row from `sites`, then ROLLBACK. Done right, the sites table survives untouched — that's the point. (patients can't be bulk-deleted at all: visits' foreign keys protect them. Constraints already saved you once today.)

hints.tier1Concept: ROLLBACK abandons everything since BEGIN. It's the safety net that makes risky maintenance survivable — practice it before you need it.

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS sites_intact FROM sites;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Maya Okonkwo (patient 1) re-registered with a new email: 'maya.k@medcore.org'. Write ONE statement that inserts patient 1 (full_name 'Maya Okonkwo') — but on a patient_id conflict, just updates the email instead. That's an UPSERT.

hints.tier1Concept: INSERT … ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE SET … is the idempotent write: insert when new, update when it already exists. excluded.col refers to the value you tried to insert.
hints.tier3Solution: INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, full_name, email) VALUES (1, 'Maya Okonkwo', 'maya.k@medcore.org') ON CONFLICT(patient_id) DO UPDATE SET email = excluded.email;

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT (SELECT email FROM patients WHERE patient_id=1) AS email, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM patients WHERE patient_id=1) AS n;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Legal revoked consent 2. Update its status to 'REVOKED' and, in the same statement, RETURN the consent_id and new status so the case file shows exactly what changed.

hints.tier1Concept: RETURNING turns a write into a read: UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT can emit the affected rows directly — no second query, no race.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
UPDATE consents
SET status = 'REVOKED'
WHERE consent_id = 2
RETURNING consent_id, ___;
hints.tier3Solution: UPDATE consents SET status = 'REVOKED' WHERE consent_id = 2 RETURNING consent_id, status;

validation.solutionQuery: UPDATE consents SET status = 'REVOKED' WHERE consent_id = 2 RETURNING consent_id, status;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Regulators demand a paper trail for contact changes. Create table `email_audit` (audit_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, patient_id INTEGER, old_email TEXT, new_email TEXT) and a trigger `trg_email_audit` that fires AFTER UPDATE OF email ON patients, inserting OLD.email and NEW.email.

hints.tier1Concept: Triggers are code that lives in the database: AFTER UPDATE OF col runs for each changed row. OLD and NEW give you both versions of the row.

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name='email_audit') AS tbl, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='trigger' AND name='trg_email_audit') AS trg;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Prove the trail works: change patient 2's email to 'ahmed.h@medcore.org'. The trigger should write the audit row for you — you only run the UPDATE.

hints.tier1Concept: Once a trigger exists, ordinary statements gain side effects. You update patients; the database writes the audit. That's the architecture working for you.
hints.tier3Solution: UPDATE patients SET email = 'ahmed.h@medcore.org' WHERE patient_id = 2;

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM email_audit WHERE patient_id = 2 AND new_email = 'ahmed.h@medcore.org') AS audited, (SELECT email FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 2) AS email;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Make impossible ages unrepresentable forever: create trigger `trg_age_guard` BEFORE UPDATE ON patients that calls RAISE(ABORT, 'age out of range') WHEN NEW.age > 120.

hints.tier1Concept: A BEFORE trigger with RAISE(ABORT, msg) vetoes a write before it happens — a programmable CHECK constraint for rules you add after the table exists.

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS trg FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='trigger' AND name='trg_age_guard' AND sql LIKE '%RAISE%';

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The analytics team keeps rewriting the same SELECT. Create view `active_roster` exposing patient_id, full_name, site and last_visit for patients whose email is present (not NULL, not empty).

hints.tier1Concept: A view is a saved query that behaves like a table. Consumers SELECT from the view; you keep one definition of 'active' in one place.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
CREATE VIEW active_roster AS
SELECT patient_id, full_name, site, last_visit
FROM patients
WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND email <> ___;
hints.tier3Solution: CREATE VIEW active_roster AS SELECT patient_id, full_name, site, last_visit FROM patients WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND email <> '';

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS v FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='view' AND name='active_roster';

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Which site is busiest? Using a CTE named `site_load` that computes visits per site (join visits to patients), return the single site with the highest visit count: site and visits. Order by visits descending, site ascending, limit 1.

hints.tier1Concept: WITH name AS (…) defines a Common Table Expression — a named intermediate result. Complex queries become readable pipelines instead of nested onions.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
WITH site_load AS (
  SELECT p.site, COUNT(*) AS visits
  FROM visits v JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = v.patient_id
  GROUP BY p.site
)
SELECT site, visits FROM site_load
ORDER BY visits DESC, site ASC
LIMIT ___;
hints.tier3Solution:
WITH site_load AS (SELECT p.site, COUNT(*) AS visits FROM visits v JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = v.patient_id GROUP BY p.site)
SELECT site, visits FROM site_load ORDER BY visits DESC, site ASC LIMIT 1;

validation.solutionQuery: WITH site_load AS (SELECT p.site, COUNT(*) AS visits FROM visits v JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = v.patient_id GROUP BY p.site) SELECT site, visits FROM site_load ORDER BY visits DESC, site ASC LIMIT 1;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: US partner sites read weight in pounds. Add a GENERATED column `weight_lb` to visits, computed as weight_kg * 2.20462 (VIRTUAL — computed on read, stored nowhere).

hints.tier1Concept: GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) VIRTUAL defines a column the database computes for you. One source of truth (kg), zero drift in the derived value.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
ALTER TABLE visits
ADD COLUMN weight_lb REAL GENERATED ALWAYS AS (___ * 2.20462) VIRTUAL;
hints.tier3Solution: ALTER TABLE visits ADD COLUMN weight_lb REAL GENERATED ALWAYS AS (weight_kg * 2.20462) VIRTUAL;

validation.verificationQuery: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sqlite_master WHERE name='visits' AND sql LIKE '%GENERATED%') AS gen, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_table_xinfo('visits') WHERE name='weight_lb') AS col;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The portal API wants JSON. For patients 1-3, return one column `payload`: a JSON object with keys 'id', 'name' and 'site' built from each row, ordered by patient_id.

hints.tier1Concept: SQLite ships JSON functions: json_object('k1', v1, 'k2', v2, …) builds an object per row. Databases can speak API directly.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT json_object('id', patient_id, 'name', full_name, 'site', ___) AS payload
FROM patients
WHERE patient_id <= 3
ORDER BY patient_id;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT json_object('id', patient_id, 'name', full_name, 'site', site) AS payload FROM patients WHERE patient_id <= 3 ORDER BY patient_id;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT json_object('id', patient_id, 'name', full_name, 'site', site) AS payload FROM patients WHERE patient_id <= 3 ORDER BY patient_id;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: The lab uploads panels as JSON arrays. Expand the array '["glucose","a1c","lipids"]' into rows using json_each — return one column `panel` with three rows.

hints.tier1Concept: json_each(json) is a table-valued function: each array element becomes a row with a `value` column. It turns embedded JSON into queryable rows.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT value AS panel
FROM json_each('["glucose","a1c","lipids"]');
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT value AS panel FROM json_each('["glucose","a1c","lipids"]');

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT value AS panel FROM json_each('["glucose","a1c","lipids"]');

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Quality gap report: per site, how many patients have NEVER had a visit? Return site and `never_seen`. LEFT JOIN patients to the distinct patient_ids in visits and count the NULLs.

hints.tier1Concept: LEFT JOIN keeps every left row, filling NULLs when the right side has no match — checking `right_col IS NULL` after it finds the gaps.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT p.site, SUM(CASE WHEN v.patient_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS never_seen
FROM patients p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT patient_id FROM visits) v ON v.patient_id = p.patient_id
GROUP BY p.___;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT p.site, SUM(CASE WHEN v.patient_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS never_seen FROM patients p LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT patient_id FROM visits) v ON v.patient_id = p.patient_id GROUP BY p.site;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT p.site, SUM(CASE WHEN v.patient_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS never_seen FROM patients p LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT patient_id FROM visits) v ON v.patient_id = p.patient_id GROUP BY p.site;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: For patients 1000-1009, show each patient's MOST RECENT visit: patient_id, visit_on and systolic. Use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_on DESC, visit_id DESC) and keep row 1 per patient. Order by patient_id.

hints.tier1Concept: 'Latest row per group' is THE window-function interview question: number rows within each partition, newest first, then filter rn = 1 in an outer query or CTE.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT patient_id, visit_on, systolic,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_on DESC, visit_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM visits
  WHERE patient_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1009
)
SELECT patient_id, visit_on, systolic FROM ranked WHERE rn = ___ ORDER BY patient_id;
hints.tier3Solution:
WITH ranked AS (SELECT patient_id, visit_on, systolic, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_on DESC, visit_id DESC) AS rn FROM visits WHERE patient_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1009)
SELECT patient_id, visit_on, systolic FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY patient_id;

validation.solutionQuery: WITH ranked AS (SELECT patient_id, visit_on, systolic, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_on DESC, visit_id DESC) AS rn FROM visits WHERE patient_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1009) SELECT patient_id, visit_on, systolic FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY patient_id;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: AUDIT WEEK, day 1. The inspector wants the enrollment story: per month ('YYYY-MM'), the new enrollments AND the running total of all enrollments to date. Order by month. (Window SUM over the monthly counts.)

hints.tier1Concept: Aggregate first (per month), then window over the aggregate: SUM(cnt) OVER (ORDER BY month) turns monthly counts into a cumulative curve.
hints.tier3Solution:
WITH monthly AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS enrolled FROM patients GROUP BY month)
SELECT month, enrolled, SUM(enrolled) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS total_to_date FROM monthly ORDER BY month;

validation.solutionQuery: WITH monthly AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS enrolled FROM patients GROUP BY month) SELECT month, enrolled, SUM(enrolled) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS total_to_date FROM monthly ORDER BY month;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Day 2: data-quality scorecard per site — site, patient count, and the percentage with a usable email (not NULL, not empty), rounded to 1 decimal. Order by the percentage descending, site ascending.

hints.tier1Concept: Conditional aggregation: AVG(CASE WHEN ok THEN 100.0 ELSE 0 END) computes a percentage in one pass — no subqueries needed.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT site, COUNT(*) AS patients,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN email IS NOT NULL AND email <> '' THEN 100.0 ELSE 0 END), 1) AS pct_contactable
FROM patients
GROUP BY site
ORDER BY pct_contactable DESC, site ASC;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT site, COUNT(*) AS patients, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN email IS NOT NULL AND email <> '' THEN 100.0 ELSE 0 END), 1) AS pct_contactable FROM patients GROUP BY site ORDER BY pct_contactable DESC, site ASC;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT site, COUNT(*) AS patients, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN email IS NOT NULL AND email <> '' THEN 100.0 ELSE 0 END), 1) AS pct_contactable FROM patients GROUP BY site ORDER BY pct_contactable DESC, site ASC;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Day 3: compliance risk. Count patients who have NO visit after '2026-03-01' (including those with no visits at all). Use NOT EXISTS.

hints.tier1Concept: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM … WHERE correlated) is the NULL-safe anti-join: 'rows with no matching row over there'. It never falls into the NOT IN + NULL trap.
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lapsed FROM patients p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM visits v WHERE v.patient_id = p.patient_id AND v.visit_on > '2026-03-01');

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lapsed FROM patients p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM visits v WHERE v.patient_id = p.patient_id AND v.visit_on > '2026-03-01');

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Day 4: safety review. List every visit with systolic of 175 or higher: the patient's full_name, the visit_on date and the systolic reading, ordered by systolic descending, then visit_on ascending, then full_name ascending.

hints.tier1Concept: A join plus a threshold filter is the everyday workhorse: connect the measurement to the person, filter, and order deterministically for the report.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
SELECT p.full_name, v.visit_on, v.systolic
FROM visits v
JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = v.patient_id
WHERE v.systolic >= ___
ORDER BY v.systolic DESC, v.visit_on ASC, p.full_name ASC;
hints.tier3Solution: SELECT p.full_name, v.visit_on, v.systolic FROM visits v JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = v.patient_id WHERE v.systolic >= 175 ORDER BY v.systolic DESC, v.visit_on ASC, p.full_name ASC;

validation.solutionQuery: SELECT p.full_name, v.visit_on, v.systolic FROM visits v JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = v.patient_id WHERE v.systolic >= 175 ORDER BY v.systolic DESC, v.visit_on ASC, p.full_name ASC;

curriculumMatrix.narrativeBriefing: Final day: the dossier. For patients 1000-1014: patient_id, full_name, site, their visit count (0 if none), and average systolic rounded to 1 decimal (NULL if no visits). Aggregate visits in a CTE, LEFT JOIN it to patients. Order by patient_id.

hints.tier1Concept: Production reports are CTE pipelines: aggregate the detail table once, LEFT JOIN it to the dimension table, and present. Every piece is something you've already built.
hints.tier2Scaffold:
WITH vis AS (
  SELECT patient_id, COUNT(*) AS visit_count, ROUND(AVG(systolic), 1) AS avg_systolic
  FROM visits GROUP BY patient_id
)
SELECT p.patient_id, p.full_name, p.site, COALESCE(v.visit_count, 0) AS visit_count, v.avg_systolic
FROM patients p LEFT JOIN vis v ON v.patient_id = p.patient_id
WHERE p.patient_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1014
ORDER BY p.patient_id;
hints.tier3Solution:
WITH vis AS (SELECT patient_id, COUNT(*) AS visit_count, ROUND(AVG(systolic), 1) AS avg_systolic FROM visits GROUP BY patient_id)
SELECT p.patient_id, p.full_name, p.site, COALESCE(v.visit_count, 0) AS visit_count, v.avg_systolic FROM patients p LEFT JOIN vis v ON v.patient_id = p.patient_id WHERE p.patient_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1014 ORDER BY p.patient_id;

examPool.prompt: How many patients are registered at each site? Return site and the count.
examPool.solutionQuery: SELECT site, COUNT(*) AS n FROM patients GROUP BY site;

examPool.prompt: Count patients whose email is missing (NULL or empty string). Return a single count.
examPool.solutionQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM patients WHERE email IS NULL OR email = '';

examPool.prompt: Find every email shared by more than one patient (exclude NULL and empty). Return email and the count of patients sharing it.
examPool.solutionQuery: SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n FROM patients WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND email <> '' GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

examPool.prompt: Return the 3 patients with the most visits: patient_id and visit count, ordered by count descending then patient_id ascending.
examPool.solutionQuery: SELECT patient_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM visits GROUP BY patient_id ORDER BY n DESC, patient_id ASC LIMIT 3;

examPool.prompt: Count enrollments per month as 'YYYY-MM', ordered by month.
examPool.solutionQuery: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS n FROM patients GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

examPool.prompt: How many patients have never had any visit? Use NOT EXISTS. Return a single count.
examPool.solutionQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM patients p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM visits v WHERE v.patient_id = p.patient_id);

examPool.prompt: For each patient from 1000 to 1004, show their most recent visit date. Return patient_id and the max visit_on, ordered by patient_id.
examPool.solutionQuery: SELECT patient_id, MAX(visit_on) AS last_visit FROM visits WHERE patient_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1004 GROUP BY patient_id ORDER BY patient_id;

examPool.prompt: What is the average systolic blood pressure across all visits, rounded to 1 decimal place?
examPool.solutionQuery: SELECT ROUND(AVG(systolic), 1) AS avg_systolic FROM visits;
